extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century reading public (The Spectator's readers); literate readers interested in manners, literature, and moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted rubrics and evaluative criteria embedded in Spectator-style essays about dancing, personal character, public office, editing texts, and conversational qualities. These are norms and standards the author uses to judge persons, arts, and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing as a method to implant good breeding and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is, I am convinced, no Method like this, to give young Women a Sense of their own Value and Dignity; and I am sure there can be none so expeditious to communicate that Value to others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dancing, properly regulated, is presented as a mechanical/artful means of instilling a sense of good breeding and virtue in young women; an example is the narrator's 'Romp' who, by dancing, displayed modesty, dignity, and the latent qualities of a modest virgin, tender wife, generous friend, kind mother. Anti-pattern: flippant, insipidly gay, wantonly forward carriage is attributed to the perverse genius of certain performers, not to the art itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good dancer requires understanding, modesty, and graceful motion
rubrics_metrics.description: "no one ever was a good Dancer, that had not a good Understanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good dancer should display modesty, becomingness, and an understanding that governs motion; grace and the 'Dignity of Aspect' command respect. Example contrasts: Mariamne (inspires respect and esteem through motion) versus Chloe (pretty but silly; her impertinent smiling shows folly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion and change of posture/aspect transform perception of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Motion, and change of Posture and Aspect, has an Effect no less surprising on the Person of Mariamne when she Dances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical motion, posture and shifting aspect can reveal or magnify innate qualities; a static portrait with many dresses is compared to the living effect of dance. Practical implication: consider movement when judging or presenting persons/figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities that command universal esteem (personal comportment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits exemplified by 'Manilius': liberal yet economical at home, plain and unaffected dress, civility that pleases all, a harmonious mixture of wit and instruction, mildness tempered by the ability to exert vigor when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who combines generosity with prudent household economy, avoids ostentation of dress, is engaging in conversation, balances gravity with humour, and is mild yet resolute, will gain universal admiration. Examples: Manilius pleases all ranks; his plain dress becomes him; his conversation is enlivened with wit and tempered with instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer in public trust should be compassionate and generous
rubrics_metrics.description: "To an honest Mind the best Perquisites of a Place are the Advantages it gives a Man of doing Good... He patronizes the Orphan and the Widow, assists the Friendless, and guides the Ignorant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those employed under great officers have frequent opportunities to exercise compassion and benevolence; they should regard poverty as a recommendation and use their position to do good within justice and equity. Practical standard: favor applicants deserving assistance even if they cannot explain claims well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament unsuited to office: roughness, pride, impatience
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Man is unfit for such a Place of Trust, who is of a sower untractable Nature... Roughness of Temper... The proud Man... The impatient Man..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials should avoid rough, proud, or impatient dispositions because such traits deter modest applicants, discourage approach, and prevent full hearing of matters. Anti-pattern: using harshness as a way to 'keep off Impertinence' is unacceptable when it causes injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a dilatory temper in office (delays are injustices)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first of these is a Dilatory Temper, which commits innumerable Cruelties without Design.... A Man who defers doing what ought to be done, is guilty of Injustice so long as he defers it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely dispatch of business is crucial; delay can inflict real harm equivalent to injustice. Criterion for judging officials: promptness and readiness to act rather than postponement for trivial motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corruption: refuse gratifications above stated fees
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no Man so improper to be employed in Business, as he who is in any degree capable of Corruption... receives more than what is the stated and unquestioned Fee of his Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corruption via gratifications, 'Dispatch Money', tokens of thankfulness, etc., is condemned; an honest man will reject such practices and prefer a moderate fortune gained with honour. Practical implication: strict refusal of extra payments is a standard of fitness for office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer men of learning for public business
rubrics_metrics.description: "It has been observed, that Men of Learning who take to Business, discharge it generally with greater Honesty than Men of the World."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men educated in liberal studies are portrayed as likelier to value virtue and be less tempted by extortion; thus employing such men in public offices will reduce corruption and produce more graceful prosperity. Hiring standard: give preference to those with learned education and virtuous training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good editorial practice for classical texts: note variants only when meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: "when a different Reading gives us a different Sense, or a new Elegance in an Author, the Editor does very well in taking Notice of it; but when he only entertains us with the several ways of spelling the same Word... they only take up the Time of the learned Reader, and puzzle the Minds of the Ignorant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should record various readings when they affect sense, metre, rhyme, or produce a new elegance; avoid cataloguing trivial orthographic or minor transcriptional variants that distract readers. Examples in practice: altering 'ever' to 'e'er' for metre, or preferring readings that preserve rhyme/sense; treat probable transcription errors (e.g., mistaking numerals) with learned caution rather than exhaustive enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a superior companion/conversationalist (Eastcourt example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eastcourt displayed 'exquisite Discerning of what was defective', an 'inimitable Faculty of telling a Story', the knack to 'raise up a pensive Temper, and mortifie an impertinently gay one', and could adapt his speech to please both refined and coarse company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great companion discerns both the ridiculous and the beautiful in objects quickly, tells stories with natural and unexpected incidents, adapts tone to the company (keeping reserve among the refined, vivacity where desired), can mimic without malice, and uses wit to correct or modulate others rather than simply to deride. Anti-patterns: being limited to supplying mere diversion and resenting being treated as only a jester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and public commendation as a tool to encourage imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Desire of Imitation may, perhaps, be a greater Incentive to the Practice of what is good, than the Aversion we may conceive at what is blameable; the one immediately directs you what you should do, whilst the other only shews you what you should avoid."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing laudatory portrayals of exemplary conduct (the 'bright Side of humane Nature') is recommended as a means to promote virtuous behaviour; represent positive examples for readers rather than only exposing vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in conversation: temper gravity with wit and preserve good humour
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Gravity of his Conversation is always enlivened with his Wit and Humour, and the Gaiety of it is tempered with something that is instructive, as well as barely agreeable.... not to be merry at the Expence of your Reason, nor serious with the Loss of your good Humour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversation should mix seriousness and amusement appropriately: wit should not undermine reason, nor seriousness destroy amiability. This balance is a criterion for judging a person's conversational virtue and social worth.
